content: H2N2 is a subtype of the Influenza A virus, which is sometimes referred to as the bird flu virus. Over time, H2N2 has undergone mutations, resulting in various strains, including the Asian Flu strain (which is now extinct in the wild), H3N2, and other strains found in avian species. It is also hypothesized that H2N2 may have been responsible for a human pandemic in 1889. The Asian Flu was a Category 2 pandemic caused by avian influenza, which emerged in China in early 1956 and persisted until 1958. This virus originated from a genetic mutation in wild ducks that combined with a pre-existing human influenza strain. The first identification of the virus occurred in Guizhou, China. It subsequently spread to Singapore in February 1957, reached Hong Kong by April, and arrived in the United States by June of the same year. The death toll in the United States was approximately 69,800. Globally, estimates of the infection rate vary significantly, ranging from 1 million to 4 million fatalities, depending on the source. The Asian Flu was caused by the H2N2 strain of Influenza A, which is classified based on the specific configuration of its hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N) surface proteins. A vaccine was developed in 1957 to mitigate the outbreak. Over time, the H2N2 strain underwent antigenic shift, evolving into the H3N2 strain, which caused a milder pandemic between 1968 and 1969. Both the H2N2 and H3N2 pandemic strains contained RNA segments derived from avian influenza viruses. Research has shown that while the 1957 (H2N2) and 1968 (H3N2) pandemic viruses arose through genetic reassortment between human and avian influenza viruses, the 1918 Spanish Flu virus appears to have been entirely derived from an avian source. Between October 2004 and February 2005, approximately 3,700 test kits containing the 1957 H2N2 virus were inadvertently distributed worldwide by the College of American Pathologists (CAP). CAP provides laboratories with unidentified viral samples to assist in accuracy testing. A private contractor, Meridian Bioscience, based in Cincinnati, USA, selected the 1957 H2N2 strain for inclusion in the kits instead of a less dangerous avian influenza subtype. According to CAP spokesperson Dr. Jared Schwartz, Meridian was aware of the virus's identity but believed it to be safe. At the time, the virus was classified as a Biosafety Level 2 (BSL-2) agent, which permitted its use in such kits. CDC Director Dr. Julie Gerberding pledged to expedite the reclassification process. The CDC collaborates with the National Institutes of Health (NIH) to determine biosafety classifications. In BSL-3 laboratories, agents are managed using specialized equipment designed to prevent airborne transmission. The 1957 H2N2 virus is considered highly lethal, prompting the U.S. government to call for the destruction of all vials containing the strain. By April 21, 2005, CDC officials reported that 99% of the distributed samples had been destroyed. On April 25, it was reported that the final remaining samples outside the United States had been destroyed at the American University of Beirut in Lebanon after being discovered at the Beirut airport. Earlier reports indicated that H2N2 samples had been sent to 3,747 laboratories under CAP's oversight and to approximately 2,700 additional laboratories certified by other organizations. Of the CAP-distributed samples, all but about 75 laboratories were located within the United States. In the United States, there is no federal regulation specifically governing the 1957 H2N2 strain. Federal officials at the CDC do not have comprehensive knowledge of how many U.S. laboratories retain this deadly strain in their viral repositories.
